newsitem.title: UK: Clarke seeks to defuse British row over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Clarke seeks to defuse British row over Europe.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, on Friday sought to defuse a row over a single European currency by writing to all 651 members of parliament setting out the government's position.

The letter from the finance minister came as Prime Minister John Major struggled to unite his fractious Conservatives in the face of a party rank-and-file revolt over demands for a full debate on Europe.

Major's hopes of winning a further term in office have been badly hurt by a row over whether three working documents related to the European Union's plans for a single currency should be examined on the floor of the House of Commons.
Major, with a parliamentary majority of just one, is anxious to avoid a debate that would doubtless reopen deep divisions over Europe that have dogged his six years as prime minister.
Clarke told MPs he wanted to set out the government's position on the three documents and sought to allay their fears of erosion of British sovereignty by the European Union.
He did not expect any legislation relating to the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) to come up for adoption when European Union finance ministers meet on December 2 in Brussels.
"At that meeting I do not expect any items of EMU legislation to come up for formal adoption. We may, however, reach a broad measure of political agreement," Clarke said.
Britain could join the EMU at any time in the future, provided the British economy met the conditions for entry.
"We are negotiating to seek to ensure that legislation binding those who join will be sensible and effective," he said.
His message was aimed at backbench MPs who fear measures will be agreed before they have had a chance to debate them.

Clarke said the results of the finance ministers' talks would be available for MPs when they hold the regular six- monthly European debate in the House of Commons before the EU heads of government meet in Dublin on December 13-14.
"That meeting is the earliest at which any binding decision could be requested," he said.

Some Conservatives with a visceral revulsion for closer European integration see the issue as a chance to promote their hostility to EMU, which is dominating the attention of governments throughout the European Union.
Egged on by the opposition parties, the "Euro-sceptics" pressed their case again on Friday under the guise of defending parliament's historic right to hold the government to account.
"Parliament should maintain its integrity and should have the opportunity to discuss these matters of absolutely crucial constitutional importance," Conservative MP John Wilkinson said.
Major, who will see a deputation of senior backbenchers next week, is hoping the scheduled debate ahead of next month's EU summit in Dublin will take the steam out of the rebellion.

Opposition politicians believe Major would lose a vote on Europe. He would then have to face a motion of no-confidence the next day which, with his one-vote majority, he should survive -- barring accidents.
